Don't install software from anywhere just because "Linux can't get viruses." It's harder to get accidental viruses, but if you install something from a bad repo, you can get infected.

Try said software in a Virtual Machine, like VirtualBox or something until you feel better with it.

Like most people I'm going to recommend Linux Mint (KDE for a standard desktop experience, or Xfce if your laptop is a bit light on resources.). If you still want to experiment with other distros, I highly recommend installing VMware or Qemu and running the experimental OS in a virtual machine on your desktop (If your laptop can handle it, it can be resource intensive). It's much more convenient when compared to dual booting.

It's important to remember that Linux is NOT a drop in replacement for Windows. It has its own ethos and way of doing things. I think that many people end up missing out on a good experience because their expectation is that Linux was a free windows replacement that would act and feel exactly like what they were use to.

Wine is still the go-to software for running windows programs in Linux. It looks like you'll have no problems running FL Studio. However, you never know how good the support really is until you actually try it. When at all possible, I highly recommend trying a native alternative, but you'll have to decide what suits your needs.

Take advantage of your distro's package management system. Having a single software repository is one of the best ideas ever, but it doesn't always meet your needs. From time to time, you may need to install something that wasn't included in your distro's default repos. Before you start downloading and compiling something, look around to see if there are extra repos that can be added that include the software you want to install.

Google is your friend. Half of experimenting with Linux is knowing how to use google to find answers. If you're having an issue or don't think that Linux can do what you want it to, chances are someone has already found a solution to it.

There are very few linux distros that actually cost anything, and if its not a corporate enviroment i'd suggest choosing from one of the thousands of free distros available.

Although i usually just suggest linux mint, you might want to check out different desktop enviroments. For example, cinnamon (the linux mint default) is a great replacement if you like the classic windows 7/xp feel. Mate is good if you want a more mac-like system. Openbox if you miss windows 95. Unity is...different. Distrowatch.com is great for finding new distros.

Wine is still king of windows compatibility, but if your a gamer you can make it easier by installing Play On Linux too.

And you should remember, packages arent universal. Fedora and Suse use .rpm packages, while debian and ubuntu use .deb packages. The two arent compatible, so if theres a program you want or need make sure you can install it. Technically, the source code should be universal, but its rarely easy.

Dont be afraid to pick up a 50 pack of dvds and try a few different distros.
